title: Joiners: Odd Fellows, Eastern Star and Knights of Columbus
bigQuestion: Why did so many Americans join lodges and orders, and what did they get from belonging?

story.title: The Envelope From the Lodge
story.kicker: In 1890, a widow in Chicago opens an envelope that will help her family get through a hard year.
paragraphs: It is 1890 in Chicago. A woman we will call Anna Becker sits at her kitchen table. Her husband, Karl, died two weeks ago. He worked in a furniture shop. Now Anna has three children and no paycheck. The rent is due soon.

Karl belonged to a lodge. Once a month he went to a meeting in a room above a store. He paid small dues every month. Anna used to tease him about the secret handshake. She did not know much about what happened at the meetings.

At the funeral, men from the lodge came in their best clothes. They wore ribbons and badges. They stood in a row by the grave. One of them shook Anna's hand. He told her the lodge would take care of its promise.

Now there is a knock at the door. A lodge officer hands Anna an envelope. Inside is a check. It will pay the rent and feed the children for many months. Anna and Karl are made-up people. But checks like this one were real, and they came to thousands of families.
story.think: What did Karl get from his lodge while he was alive? What did his family get after he died?

lessons.title: One Man in Three
lessons.mainIdea: In the late 1800s and early 1900s, joining a lodge or order was one of the most common things an American adult did.
reading: Walk down a main street in an American town around 1900. You might see a lodge hall above the bank. You might see a sign for the Odd Fellows, the Masons or the Woodmen. Almost every town had several lodges. Big cities had hundreds.

Historian David Beito studied these groups. He *estimates* that about one in three adult men belonged to a lodge around 1910. He says that number is probably low. Many men belonged to more than one *order*. An order is a large club with many local lodges.

These groups had secret handshakes and ceremonies. But the lodges themselves were not hidden. They printed their names in newspapers. They marched in parades. They carved their names on buildings. The ritual was private, but the group was public.

words.d: makes a careful guess about a number using the evidence you have
a large club or society with many local lodges that share the same rules
a ceremony with set words and actions done the same way each time

look.title: A Historian's Estimate
look.text: Beito estimates that around 1910, about one in three adult American men belonged to a fraternal lodge. He calls this a conservative estimate, meaning the true number may have been higher.
look.cite: David T. Beito, From Mutual Aid to the Welfare State: Fraternal Societies and Social Services, 1890-1967 (University of North Carolina Press, 2000)
look.prompt: If a street had 30 grown men, about how many would belong to a lodge by Beito's estimate?

check.q: About how many adult men belonged to a lodge around 1910, by Beito's estimate?
check.why: Beito estimates about one in three adult men belonged to a lodge around 1910.

check.q: What is an order?
choices: A large club with many local lodges
check.why: The reading says an order is a large club with many local lodges.

check.q: Which part of lodge life was usually kept private?
check.why: The reading says the ritual was private, but the group was public.

lessons.title: Help Before Insurance
lessons.mainIdea: Many lodges gave mutual aid, such as sick pay, burial money and life insurance, before most families could buy insurance.
reading: In 1890, most workers had no sick pay. If a worker got hurt, the paychecks stopped. If he died, his family could lose their home. There was no Social Security yet. Few families could buy insurance from a company.

Lodges filled this gap with *mutual aid*. Mutual aid means members help each other. Each member paid small *dues*. The lodge saved the money. When a member was sick, the lodge paid him. When he died, the lodge helped pay for the funeral.

Some orders went further and sold life insurance. In 1868, the Ancient Order of United Workmen began in Meadville, Pennsylvania. Historians call it the first fraternal life insurance order. Many other orders soon copied the idea.

words.d: when members of a group help each other, often by sharing money in hard times
small regular payments that members give to their club
a plan where people pay a little money now to get help if something bad happens later

look.title: The Class Jar
look.text: Twenty students each put one coin in a class jar every week. After a while, the jar is full. One day a student's backpack is torn and her books are ruined. The class uses money from the jar to help her buy new ones. Next month, it might help someone else.
look.prompt: How is the class jar like a lodge's mutual aid? Why does it work better when many people join?

check.q: What does mutual aid mean?
choices: One rich person pays for all
check.why: The reading says mutual aid means members help each other.

check.q: Why did lodge help matter so much in 1890?
choices: Everyone had sick pay at work
The lodges were run by the government
Most workers had no sick pay or insurance
check.why: The reading says most workers had no sick pay, and there was no Social Security yet.

check.q: What was special about the Ancient Order of United Workmen?
choices: It was the first Masonic lodge
Historians call it the first fraternal life insurance order
check.why: The reading says historians call it the first fraternal life insurance order.

lessons.title: The Odd Fellows
lessons.mainIdea: The Odd Fellows began in America in 1819 and promised to care for sick members, widows and orphans.
reading: On April 26, 1819, five men met at the Seven Stars Tavern in Baltimore, Maryland. Their leader was Thomas Wildey. He had come from England, where Odd Fellows lodges already met. The five men started the first Odd Fellows lodge in America.

The Odd Fellows promised to visit the sick, help people in trouble, bury the dead and teach orphans. Their *symbol* is three links of a chain. The links stand for Friendship, Love and Truth. You can still see the three links on old buildings.

In 1851, the Odd Fellows added the Rebekah degree for women. Schuyler Colfax, who later became Vice President, pushed for it. A *degree* is a level of membership with its own ceremony. Women now had their own place in the order.

words.d: a picture or shape that stands for an idea
a level of membership in an order, reached through its own ceremony

look.title: Three Links on a Wall

look.prompt: Which order used this symbol? What does each letter stand for?

check.q: What do the three links of the Odd Fellows stand for?
check.why: The reading says the links stand for Friendship, Love and Truth.

check.q: What did the Rebekah degree do?
choices: It gave women a place in the Odd Fellows
It made the order a bank
It moved the order to England
check.why: The reading says the Rebekah degree, added in 1851, gave women their own place in the order.

lessons.title: The Order of the Eastern Star
lessons.mainIdea: The Order of the Eastern Star is an order that women and men join together, built on the stories of five heroines.
reading: In the winter of 1849 to 1850, Rob Morris lived in Mississippi. He was a Mason. He wrote a ceremony for the wives, daughters, mothers and sisters of Masons. It became the start of the Order of the *Eastern Star*.

The order's symbol is a star with five points. Each point honors a *heroine*, a woman admired for her goodness. Most come from Bible stories, such as Ruth and Esther. Their stories teach values like loyalty and faith. Women and Masons join together in a *chapter*.

In November 1876, chapters met in Indianapolis and formed one national body. Its first leader was Elizabeth Butler of Illinois. In 1890, the order printed its full ceremony as a book. Anyone can read it today. Secret often meant private, not hidden.

words.d: an order that women and Masons join together, with a five-pointed star as its symbol
a woman admired for her courage or goodness
a local group of the Eastern Star, like a lodge

look.title: Five Points, Five Stories
look.text: Picture a large star with five points. Each point has its own color. Each point also stands for a heroine, most from Bible stories. A new member hears each story in turn. Each one teaches a different value, like loyalty or faith.

check.q: What does each point of the Eastern Star stand for?
choices: A state in the United States

check.why: The reading says each point honors a heroine, and most come from Bible stories, such as Ruth and Esther.

check.q: Who can join the Eastern Star?
check.why: The reading says women and Masons can join and meet together in a chapter.

lessons.title: Father McGivney's Idea
lessons.mainIdea: Father Michael McGivney started the Knights of Columbus to help Catholic men care for their families.
reading: In the 1880s, Father Michael McGivney was a young *priest* at St. Mary's Church in New Haven, Connecticut. Many people in his church worked hard jobs for low pay. When a father died, his family could fall into deep trouble fast.

Catholics had few lodges of their own. The Catholic Church told its members not to join the Masons. Many other orders felt Protestant in their prayers and customs. So Catholic men were often left out of the help that lodges gave.

Father McGivney had an idea. Catholic men could form their own order. They could pay dues and protect each other's families. They could also share their faith. In October 1881, a small group of men met with him to begin.

words.d: a leader in the Catholic Church who leads worship and cares for a church's people
a Christian who belongs to one of the churches that split from the Catholic Church

check.why: The reading says he was a priest at St. Mary's Church in New Haven.

check.q: Why were Catholic men often left out of lodge help?
choices: They did not want any help

check.why: The reading says the Church told members not to join the Masons, and many orders felt Protestant.

check.q: What was one goal of Father McGivney's new order?
check.why: The reading says the men could pay dues and protect each other's families.

lessons.title: Chartered in 1882
lessons.mainIdea: Connecticut chartered the Knights of Columbus in 1882, and the order soon spread to other states, including Illinois.
reading: On March 29, 1882, the Connecticut legislature gave the new group a charter. Now it was official. The men named it the Knights of Columbus, after Christopher Columbus. They wanted to show that Catholics had long been part of America's story.

The order sold life insurance to its members. If a Knight died, his widow received money. Members also did *charity*, which means giving help to people in need. Each local group of Knights is called a *council*.

The order grew fast. In 1896, Chicago Council No. 182 became the first council in Illinois. Councils later spread to many other countries. Today Knights of Columbus councils still meet in parishes across the United States.

words.d: giving money, time or help to people who need it
a local group of the Knights of Columbus

lessons.title: Tree-Stump Gravestones
lessons.mainIdea: The Woodmen of the World once gave members gravestones carved like tree stumps as part of their insurance.
reading: Walk through an old cemetery in the Midwest or South. You may find a gravestone carved to look like a cut tree stump. It may show an axe or a log. Many of these stones belonged to members of the Woodmen of the World.

Joseph Cullen Root started the Woodmen of the World in Omaha, Nebraska, in 1890. It was a *fraternal* insurance order. Members paid dues. When a member died, the order paid his family. It also gave a gravestone, called a *marker*.

At first the tree-stump markers were free. Later, members had to pay extra, about $100, to get one. The program stopped in the 1920s. Many stones carry the Latin motto Dum Tacet Clamat. It means "Though silent, he speaks."

words.d: like brothers; used for clubs whose members treat each other as family
a stone or sign that shows where a person is buried

look.title: A Promise in Stone
look.text: In 1892, the Woodmen announced that a monument would be placed on the grave of every member who had kept up with his payments.
look.cite: Woodmen of the World, Pacific Jurisdiction announcement, 1892, as described in Annette Stott, "The Woodmen of the World Monument Program," Markers XX (2003)
look.prompt: What did a member have to do to get a monument? Why might this promise help the order find new members?

check.q: Who started the Woodmen of the World?
check.why: The reading says Joseph Cullen Root started it in Omaha in 1890.

choices: A stone that shows where a person is buried
check.why: The reading says the gravestone was called a marker.

check.q: What does Dum Tacet Clamat mean?
check.why: The reading says the Latin motto means "Though silent, he speaks."

lessons.title: A Skyscraper With Lodge Rooms
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Masonic Temple, finished in 1892, was a skyscraper with shops below and lodge rooms at the top.
reading: On November 6, 1890, a parade marched through downtown Chicago. Masons came to lay the *cornerstone* of a new building. A cornerstone is a special first stone set in a public ceremony. The building rose at State and Randolph streets.

The Masonic Temple was finished in 1892. The architects were Burnham and Root. It stood about 302 feet tall, with about 21 stories. Shops filled the lower floors. Offices filled the middle. Lodge rooms were near the top.

People at the time called it the tallest building in the world. That claim is *disputed*. A New York building was taller if you count its tower. But the Masonic Temple became Chicago's tallest in 1895. It was torn down in 1939.

words.d: a special first stone of a building, set in place during a public ceremony
argued about, because people disagree about whether it is true

look.title: A Printed Program for a Parade
look.text: A printed program from November 6, 1890, lists the ceremonies for laying the cornerstone of the Masonic Fraternity Temple in Chicago. It also gives instructions for the parade.
look.cite: Ceremonies of Laying the Cornerstone of the Masonic Fraternity Temple, program, 1890 (Scottish Rite Masonic Museum and Library)
look.prompt: Does this program show a group hiding, or a group being public? What clue tells you?

check.q: Where did Chicago's Masonic Temple stand?
check.why: The reading says the building rose at State and Randolph streets.

check.q: What was on the top floors of the Masonic Temple?
check.why: The reading says lodge rooms were near the top, with shops and offices below.

check.q: Why is the claim of tallest in the world called disputed?
choices: A New York building was taller if you count its tower
check.why: The reading says a New York building was taller if you count its tower.

lessons.title: Medinah Temple and a Hospital
lessons.mainIdea: Chicago's Shriners built Medinah Temple in 1912 and later helped open a hospital for children.
reading: The *Shriners* are an order whose members are also Masons. They are known for parades, bright red hats called fezzes and fun. In Chicago, their group was called Medinah Temple.

In 1912, the Chicago Shriners finished a grand building at 600 North Wabash Avenue. It was also called Medinah Temple. It had domes and fancy brick patterns. Its hall held about 4,200 people. In 2000, Chicago named it an official city *landmark*.

The Shriners also cared about children. In 1926, a Shriners hospital for children opened in Chicago. Members of Medinah Temple had decided to build it. The first Shriners hospital had opened in Shreveport, Louisiana, in 1922.

words.d: an order of Masons known for parades, red fez hats and children's hospitals
a building a city protects because it is important to its history

lessons.title: Critics and Changing Times
lessons.mainIdea: Some Americans criticized secret orders, and after the 1950s, far fewer people joined them.
reading: Not everyone liked lodges. In 1868, a group called the National Christian Association began. Jonathan Blanchard of Wheaton College in Illinois was a leader. He and other *critics* said secret oaths did not fit with their Christian faith. Their newspaper was printed in Chicago.
Lodge members saw things differently. They said their oaths were promises of friendship and help. Both sides were sincere. You can read what each side wrote and decide for yourself.

Later, a different change came. After the 1950s, far fewer Americans joined lodges. Political scientist Robert Putnam counted this *decline*. He argued people were joining fewer groups. Other scholars say people found new ways to meet and help.

words.d: people who point out what they think is wrong with something
a drop or fall in number over time

look.title: Fewer Members Over Time
look.cite: Robert D. Putnam, "Bowling Alone: America's Declining Social Capital," Journal of Democracy (1995)
